documentNotes.title: INSTRUCTIONS
documentNotes.statement:
4 Questions, 60 minutes

DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example,

  Doe, Jamie
  Q1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. Cell phones may not be used during the exam or while the exam papers are present. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Each of the four questions is worth 25 points. The questions are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Good luck!

documentNotes.title: Solutions to Problems
documentNotes.statement: *Any correct solution should be awarded equivalent points. Suggested partial-credit points are presented in square brackets at the right margin. You may further break down the listed points into one point increments. If it is clear they have done an intermediate step, they should get credit for it even if they have not presented it. For example, in 4.a., if a student wrote down $\omega = (Mv\alpha L)/(2mL^2)$, they should get 6 points credit. Students should not be penalized in a subsequent part for using the wrong answer to a previous part. (No double jeopardy.)*

problems.title: Acceleration vs. Time
problems.statement: An object starts at rest at the origin at $t = 0$ and accelerates according to the graph shown above. The motion is one-dimensional.

figures.caption: Acceleration vs. Time
figures.alt: Graph of acceleration a versus time t: a = a0 from 0 to t0, a = 0 from t0 to 2t0, a = –a0 after 2t0. Axis labels a, t; tick labels a0, –a0, t0, 2t0; title Acceleration vs. Time.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Sketch a graph of velocity versus time. Show and clearly label all extreme values, discontinuities, and zero crossings.

answer.note: Velocity rises linearly to a0t0 at t0, stays constant to 2t0, then decreases linearly, crossing zero at 3t0.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: At what time (expressed in terms of $t_0$) does the object return to the origin?

solution.statement:
**1. a.** The graph should look like the following.

Both axes are labeled [1]

Shows $v = 0$ at $t = 0$ [1]

Straight line with positive slope from $t = 0$ to $t = t_0$ [1]

Shows discontinuity in slope at $t = t_0$ [1]

Labels maximum velocity at $v = a_0t_0$ [1]

Shows constant velocity from $t = t_0$ to $t = 2t_0$ [1]

Shows discontinuity in slope at $t = 2t_0$ [1]

Straight line with negative slope after $t = 2t_0$ [1]

Shows $v = 0$ at $t = 3t_0$ [1]

No spurious features shown [1]

*(There are at least two methods that can be used to find the time at which the object returns to the origin. These are detailed below. Students may be awarded points from only one method.)*

**b.** Method I: The distance traveled is given by the area under the velocity vs. time curve. [5]

Continue the curve until the total area is zero, i.e., the area below the $t$-axis is equal to the area above it. Find the value of $t$ at which the object returns to the origin either by construction or geometrical formula. The construction method follows.

The area above the time axis is $d_+ = 2a_0t_0^{\,2}$. [4]

To make the area below the axis equal, extend the graph $2t_0$ beyond the zero crossing at $3t_0$. [4]

and $t = 2t_0 + 3t_0 = 5t_0$ [2]

*(Students should be given full credit for any valid geometrical argument.)*

Method II: For the interval $t = 0$ to $t = t_0$, $a = +a_0$ and $v_0 = 0$. The kinematic equations for motion with constant acceleration yield

At time $t = t_0$, $v = a_0t_0$ [2]

$x = \frac{1}{2}a_0t_0^{\,2}$. [2]

These become the initial velocity and displacement for the next interval $t = t_0$ to $t = 2t_0$. During this interval, $a = 0$ and $v_0 = a_0t_0$.

At time $t = 2t_0$, $v = a_0t_0$ [2]

$x = x_0 + v_0(2t_0 - t_0) = \frac{1}{2}a_0t_0^{\,2} + (a_0t_0)t_0 = \frac{3}{2}a_0t_0^{\,2}$. [2]

These become the initial velocity and displacement for the next interval $t > 2t_0$. During this interval, $a = -a_0$ and $v_0 = a_0t_0$.

For $t > 2t_0$, $x = x_0 + v_0(t - 2t_0) - \frac{1}{2}a_0(t - 2t_0)^2 = \frac{3}{2}a_0t_0^{\,2} + a_0t_0(t - 2t_0) - \frac{1}{2}a_0(t - 2t_0)^2$ [4]

$x = \frac{1}{2}a_0[3t_0 - (t - 2t_0)][t_0 + (t - 2t_0)] = \frac{1}{2}a_0(5t_0 - t)(t - t_0)$

It returns to the origin when $x = 0$. This happens at $t = 5t_0$. [3]

The other solution is eliminated because the equation is only valid in the time interval $t > 2t_0$.

figures.caption: Velocity vs. Time
figures.alt: Velocity v versus time t: v rises linearly from 0 to a0t0 at t0, stays constant until 2t0, then decreases linearly, crossing zero at 3t0 and continuing negative past 4t0. Labels v, t, a0t0, t0, 2t0, 3t0, 4t0.

Construction on the velocity graph: the triangle above the axis (area under the curve up to 2t0) is moved by a curved arrow; shaded area above the axis equals shaded triangle below the axis. Dimension arrows 2t0 and 3t0 along the axis and 2t0 beyond the zero crossing; axes v and t.

problems.statement: One means of attempting to detect planets orbiting other stars is to look for stellar wobble. This wobble indicates motion of the star about the star-planet center of mass. Assume the mass of the star is $M$, the mass of the planet $\alpha M$ ($\alpha \ll 1$), and the distance from the center of the star to the center of the planet is $R$. See accompanying diagram.

figures.alt: A large circle labelled M (star) and a small circle labelled αM (planet), joined by a double-headed arrow labelled R between their centers.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Derive an equation for the magnitude of the star’s velocity $v$ about the star-planet center of mass in terms of $\alpha$, $G$, $M$, and $R$. Your answer should be given to lowest order in $\alpha$.
parts.statementAfter: Scientists think they can detect stars with speeds $v$ as small as $3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the maximum distance a planet with Earth’s mass could be from a star of solar mass and still be detected by stellar wobble? Express your answer in astronomical units (A.U.).

problems.statementAfterParts:
Possibly useful information:

| | |
|---|---|
| Mass of sun | $2.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg}$ |
| $\alpha$ for Earth | $3.0\times10^{-6}$ |
| $R$ for Earth | $1.5\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m}$ (= 1 A.U.) |

solution.statement:
**2. a.** To find the center of mass of the star planet system, divide the distance $R$ into $R - x$ and $x$ as shown in the diagram. Placing the origin at the center of mass, the general center of mass equation $M_{tot}x_{cm} = m_1x_1 + m_2x_2$ becomes $0 = Mx - \alpha M(R - x)$.

Solving for $x$, the center of star to center of mass distance. $x = \frac{\alpha R}{1 + \alpha}$. [5]

Using Newton’s Second Law to describe the star’s motion $\sum F = Ma$ [2]

The net force is the universal gravitational force $F = G\frac{M\alpha M}{R^2}$ [3]

*(Maximum of [2] if $x$ is used in place of $R$.)*

For uniform motion in a circle of radius $x$ about the center of mass, $a = \frac{v^2}{x}$. [3]

*(Maximum of [2] if $R$ is used in place of $x$.)*

Substituting for $x$, this becomes $a = \frac{(1 + \alpha)v^2}{\alpha R}$ [1]

Combining these equations $G\frac{M\alpha M}{R^2} = M\left(\frac{(1 + \alpha)v^2}{\alpha R}\right)$ [2]

Canceling common factors $G\frac{\alpha M}{R} = \frac{(1 + \alpha)v^2}{\alpha}$. [1]

Solving for $v$ $v = \sqrt{\frac{G\alpha^2M}{R(1 + \alpha)}}$. [1]

To lowest order in $\alpha$ this is $v \approx \alpha\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R}}$ [2] *(Exact answer required.)*

**b.** Solving for $R$ $R \approx \frac{\alpha^2GM}{v^2}$ [2]

Inserting the values given with the problem

$$R \approx \frac{(3\times10^{-6})^2(6.67\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2})(2.0\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{kg})}{(3.0\ \mathrm{m/s})^2} = 1.33\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$$ [2]

Converting to A.U. $R \approx 8.9\times10^{-4}$ A.U. [1]

figures.alt: Star circle labelled M and planet circle labelled αM; the line between their centers is divided into x (from the star center to the center of mass) and R-x (from the center of mass to the planet).

problems.statement: A uniform board of mass $m$ and length $L$ is placed on the back of a flatbed truck as shown in the diagram above. There is no friction between the top of the board and the vertical surface of the truck. The coefficient of static friction between the bottom of the board and the horizontal surface of the truck is $\mu_s = 0.50$. The truck always moves in the forward direction. Express your answers to the following as multiples of $g$.

figures.alt: Side view of a flatbed truck with two wheels and a cab on the right; a board of length L leans from the flatbed against the vertical back of the cab. Its top is 0.8 L above the bed and its foot is 0.6 L from the cab wall.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the maximum starting acceleration the truck can have if the board is not to slip or fall over?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is the maximum stopping acceleration the truck can have if the board is not to slip or fall over?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: For what value of stopping acceleration is the static frictional force equal to zero?

solution.statement:
**3. a.** Method I: (Inertial reference frame) The accompanying diagram shows the forces acting when the truck is accelerating to the right. The force of static friction must be to the right to provide the board’s acceleration.

There is no acceleration in the $y$-direction, so the sum of forces in that direction must equal zero.

$\sum F_y = N - mg = 0$. [2]

In the $x$-direction, Newton’s Second Law yields

$\sum F_x = f - P = ma$. [2]

There is no rotation about the center of mass (the center of the board), so the net torque about that point must equal zero. *(This is not true for all points. The condition that the net torque must be zero about any axis applies only when the object is in static equilibrium, i.e., not accelerating.)*

$\sum \tau = P(0.4L) + f(0.4L) - N(0.3L) = 0$. [3]

Solving for $P$ $P = 0.75N - f$.

Substituting into the $F_x$ equation

$f - (0.75N - f) = 2f - 0.75N = ma$.

The acceleration is maximum when $f$ takes on its maximum value $f_{max} = \mu_sN$ [2]

$ma_{max} = 2f_{max} - 0.75N = 2\mu_sN - 0.75N = (2\mu_s - 0.75)mg$

or $a_{max} = (2(0.5) - 0.75)g = 0.25g$ [1]

**a.** Method II: (Accelerating reference frame attached to truck) The accompanying diagram shows the forces acting when the truck is accelerating to the right. The force of static friction must be to the right to balance the other forces. There is no acceleration in the $y$-direction, so the sum of forces in that direction must equal zero.

$\sum F_y = N - mg = 0$. [2]

In the $x$-direction, Newton’s First Law yields

$\sum F_x = f - P - ma = 0$. [2]

There is no rotation. In this frame any axis works. Selecting the bottom of the board.

$\sum \tau = P(0.8L) + ma(0.4L) - mg(0.3L) = 0$ [3]

Solving for $P$ $P = 0.375mg - 0.50ma$.

Substituting into the $F_x$ equation

$f - (0.375mg - 0.50ma) - ma = f - 0.375mg - 0.50ma = 0$.

The acceleration is maximum when $f$ takes on its maximum value $f_{max} = \mu_sN = \mu_smg$ [2]

$ma_{max} = 2f_{max} - 0.75mg = 2\mu_smg - 0.75mg = (2\mu_s - 0.75)mg$

or $a_{max} = (2(0.5) - 0.75)g = 0.25g$ [1]

*(While we only present this method for Part (a), it can be used for Parts (b) and (c) as well.)*

**b.** For maximum acceleration in the stopping case, $f$ must be in the same direction as the acceleration. The equations become

$\sum F_y = N - mg = 0$ [2]

$\sum F_x = f + P = ma$ [2]

$\sum \tau = P(0.4L) - f(0.4L) - N(0.3L) = 0$ [3]

Solving for $P$ $P = 0.75N + f$

Substituting into the $F_x$ equation

$f + (0.75N + f) = 2f + 0.75N = ma$.

The acceleration is maximum when $f$ takes on its maximum value $f_{max} = \mu_sN$ [2]

$ma_{max} = 2f_{max} + 0.75N = 2\mu_sN + 0.75N = (2\mu_s + 0.75)mg$

or $a_{max} = (2(0.5) + 0.75)g = 1.75g$ [1]

**c.** If $f = 0$ in the Part b case, $P = ma$ [2]

and $P = 0.75N = 0.75mg$ [2]

Combining $a = 0.75g$ [1]

figures.alt: Free-body diagram of the board (Method I, truck accelerating to the right): P pointing left at the top, N upward and f to the right at the bottom, mg downward at the center; the top is 0.8 L above the bed and the foot is 0.6 L from the wall.

Free-body diagram of the board in the truck frame (Method II): P to the left at the top, ma to the left at the center, mg downward, N upward and f to the right at the bottom; dimensions 0.8 L and 0.6 L.
Free-body diagram of the board for the stopping case: P to the left at the top, mg downward, N upward and f to the left at the bottom; dimensions 0.8 L and 0.6 L.

problems.statement: A dumbbell of length $2L$ is initially at rest on a horizontal surface. The accompanying diagram shows a view looking down at the surface. Both cubes at the ends of the dumbbell have mass $m$. The connecting rod is massless. An object with mass $M$ and velocity $v$ perpendicular to the rod slides across the surface and strikes the dumbbell a distance $\alpha L$ from its center. The collision is perfectly elastic. There is no friction between any of the objects and the surface. Assume the masses $M$ and $m$ can be treated as point masses. After the collision, mass $M$ is at rest.

figures.alt: Top view: a vertical rod with a cube m at each end; dashed dimension arrows L and L from the center to each end. A cube M on the left moves right with velocity v toward the rod, striking it a distance αL below the center.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find $M$ in terms of some or all of the quantities $\alpha$, $L$, $v$, and $m$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: What is $M$ if $\alpha = 1$, i.e., $M$ strikes $m$ at the end of the rod?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: What is $M$ if $\alpha = 0$, i.e., $M$ strikes at the center of the rod?

problems.statementAfterParts: Note: Parts (b) and (c) can be answered without first doing Part (a).

solution.statement:
**4.** Before the collision the dumbbell is at rest and mass $M$ moves with velocity $v$. After the collision $M$ is at rest and the dumbbell is both translating and rotating. Let $v_{cm}$ equal the translational velocity of the dumbbell center of mass and let $\omega$ equal the angular velocity of the dumbbell about its center of mass.

The moment of inertia of the dumbbell about its center of mass is $I = 2mL^2$ [2]

Angular momentum is conserved. The initial angular momentum of $M$ about the dumbbell’s center of mass equals the final angular momentum of the dumbbell about its center of mass.

$Mv(\alpha L) = I\omega$ [3]

Solving for $\omega$ $\omega = \frac{Mv\alpha L}{I} = \frac{Mv\alpha L}{2mL^2} = \frac{Mv\alpha}{2mL}$ [1]

Linear momentum is conserved. $Mv = 2mv_{cm}$ [3]

Solving for the center of mass velocity $v_{cm} = \frac{Mv}{2m}$. [1]

The collision is elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved.

$\frac{1}{2}Mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2m)v_{cm}^{\,2} + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ [3]

Substituting into this equation $Mv^2 = (2m)\left(\frac{Mv}{2m}\right)^2 + (2mL^2)\left(\frac{Mv\alpha}{2mL}\right)^2$ [1]

Simplifying $1 = \frac{M}{2m} + \frac{M\alpha^2}{2m} = \frac{M}{2m}(1 + \alpha^2)$

Therefore $M = \frac{2m}{1 + \alpha^2}$ [1]

**b.** If $\alpha = 1$ $M = \frac{2m}{1 + 1} = m$ [5]

(Immediately after the collision the lower mass $m$ has speed $v$. $M$ and the other $m$ are at rest. This conserves mechanical energy, linear momentum, and angular momentum.)

**c.** If $\alpha = 0$ $M = \frac{2m}{1 + 0} = 2m$ [5]

(Immediately after the collision both masses $m$ have speed $v$. This conserves mechanical energy and linear momentum. Angular momentum about the center of mass is zero in this case.)
